name: Chichicapan Zapotec
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Glaser, Barbara, H. Andrew Black & Joseph P. Benton. 1997. Modeling Chichicapan Zapotec morphology. SIL Mexico Workpapers 12: 11-33 (Glottolog hhtype: phonology). sil.org returns 403.

new_statements.quote: Acento de intensidad: en la primera sílaba de la última raíz de una palabra; no es predecible en términos fonológicos puesto que una raíz puede tener una o dos sílabas en palabras nativas –más en préstamos– y puede llevar prefijos léxicos que no aceptan el acento (un signo de más, +, aparece antes de la sílaba tónica en los ejemplos cuando el acento no recae en la primera)
new_statements.translation: Intensity (dynamic) stress: on the first syllable of the last root of a word; it is not predictable in phonological terms, since a root may have one or two syllables in native words – more in loanwords – and may carry lexical prefixes that do not accept stress (a plus sign, +, appears before the stressed syllable in the examples when the stress does not fall on the first one).
new_statements.citation: Smith Stark, Thomas C. 2007. Los préstamos entre el español y el zapoteco de San Baltasar Chichicapan. UniverSOS: Revista de Lenguas Indígenas y Universos Culturales 4: 9-39. §2.2 'Los sistemas fonológicos del español y del zapoteco', example (5).
new_statements.locator: p. 18 (PDF page 18 of the whole-issue file; example (5) under §2.2)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is morphologically anchored: it falls on the first syllable of the last (rightmost) root of the word; prefixes (including lexical prefixes) and any non-final root in a compound are unstressed. Because roots are 1-2 syllables (longer in Spanish loans) and prefixes vary, the position is not computable from the phonological string alone. Corroborated first-hand by Benton, Black & Glaser 1997 (SIL-Mexico Workpapers 12), p. 25: 'the initial nucleus of a root will reduce (in stress and/or glottalization) if the root is not the final root in the word', and p. 29: 'When it occurs as the first member of a compound, a noun can have an unstressed allomorph'. The language is also tonal (Smith-Stark 2007 p. 18: tones grave, ascendente, descendente; Benton 1987 p. 72 lists six tones), with stress a separate 'acento de intensidad'.
new_statements.exceptions: Smith-Stark 2007: position is 'no predecible en términos fonológicos' because root length varies and lexical prefixes do not take stress; in the loanword examples stress is marked with + before the tonic syllable whenever it is not word-initial (e.g. ga+mízhi 'camisa', pa+râje 'paraje', sacra+shtân 'sacristán'). Glaser/Black/Benton 1997: non-final roots in compounds have reduced, 'unstressed' allomorphs (e.g. tu'h 'rope' > tu'-kusi'w 'lightning'; naan 'lady' > nan-:swehktya 'mother-in-law').
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root + prefixes; compounds); statement made in a phoneme-inventory sketch preceding a loanword study, not an instrumental study. The Glaser/Black/Benton 1997 evidence is from an AMPLE morphological-parser description (tone-and-stress table (2), pp. 11-12; allomorphy pp. 25, 29).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Zapotec of San Baltazar Chichicapan (official spelling San Baltazar Chichicápam), district of Ocotlán, Oaxaca = chic1274 exactly; Smith-Stark places it among the 'dialectos vallistas del zapoteco central'. No dialect split involved.

sources.note: p. 18, §2.2 ex. (5): 'Acento de intensidad: en la primera sílaba de la última raíz de una palabra; no es predecible en términos fonológicos...' (stress on the first syllable of the last root; lexical prefixes unstressed; + marks a non-initial tonic syllable in examples). Also tones grave/ascendente/descendente and four laryngealization types; refers to Smith Stark 2003b for detail.

sources.citation: Benton, Joe, Andy Black & Barbara Glaser [Glottolog: Glaser, Black & Benton]. 1997. Modeling Chichicapan Zapotec morphology. SIL-Mexico Workpapers 12: 11-33.
sources.note: §1 'Sound system', table (2) 'Chichicapan tone and stress' (pp. 11-12): vowel-letter conventions mark tone, stress and glottalization together ('v rising tone with stress', 'vh low tone with stress',...). p. 25: 'the initial nucleus of a root will reduce (in stress and/or glottalization) if the root is not the final root in the word. Such allomorphs are labeled unstressed'. p. 29: a noun as first member of a compound 'can have an unstressed allomorph'. No explicit rule for stress position within the root. Scanned image PDF (Wayback copy of the old SIL Mexico scan), scanned at 300 dpi.

sources.citation: Benton, Joseph. 1987. Clause and sentence-level word order and discourse strategy in Chichicapan Zapotec oral narrative discourse. SIL-Mexico Workpapers 9: 72-84.
sources.note: Footnote p. 72 gives the phoneme inventory and 'suprasegmental features, of which there are three types: tones... low, high, low-rising, high-rising, low-falling, and high-falling; glottalization V', and syllable types high-intensity (Vh) and low-intensity (VV)'. Nothing on stress placement.
